sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: Axis, chamber hypertrophy and bundle-branch blocks

sections.body: Four syndromes are diagnosed, or at least strongly suspected, from the end of the bed: **heart failure** (congestion and perfusion), **cardiac tamponade** (a medical emergency), **constrictive pericarditis** (a chronic mimic of right heart failure and liver disease) and **infective endocarditis** (fever plus a murmur plus peripheral stigmata). The exam tests the eponyms and, above all, the difference between tamponade and constriction.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
### Heart failure

- **Congestion ("wet")**: raised JVP (the most useful single sign of raised filling pressure), positive abdominojugular test, orthopnoea, lung crackles, pleural effusions (often right-sided or bilateral), hepatomegaly, ascites, sacral and leg oedema.
- **Perfusion ("cold")**: cool clammy peripheries, narrow pulse pressure (proportional pulse pressure under about 25%), hypotension, confusion, oliguria.
- **The heart**: displaced apex, **S3** (the most specific sign of LV dysfunction after middle age), functional MR, **pulsus alternans** in severe systolic dysfunction; Cheyne-Stokes breathing.

| Profile | Congestion | Perfusion | Usual therapy direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warm and dry | No | Adequate | Optimise oral therapy |
| Warm and wet | Yes | Adequate | Diuretics (with vasodilators if hypertensive) |
| Cold and wet | Yes | Low | Inotropes/vasopressors as needed, then diuretics; consider mechanical support |
| Cold and dry | No | Low | Cautious fluids, look for hypovolaemia |

### Cardiac tamponade

- **Beck triad**: **hypotension, raised JVP, quiet (muffled) heart sounds**; classic for **acute** tamponade (trauma, ventricular rupture, aortic dissection), less complete in slowly accumulating effusions.
- Tachycardia, **pulsus paradoxus**, raised JVP with an **absent y descent**, clear lungs.
- Large effusion: impalpable apex, **Ewart sign** (dullness and bronchial breathing below the left scapula from lung compression).

[[figure:pe-pulse-paradoxus]]

[[figure:pe-jvp-tamponade-absent-y]]

### Constrictive pericarditis

- Raised JVP with a **steep y descent** (Friedreich sign) and an M/W contour, **Kussmaul sign**, **pericardial knock**, hepatomegaly and **ascites out of proportion to leg oedema**; pulsus paradoxus is uncommon or mild.
- Causes: tuberculosis (still the leading cause where TB is endemic), previous cardiac surgery, radiotherapy, viral/idiopathic pericarditis.

[[figure:pe-jvp-constrictive-y-descent]]

[[figure:pe-jvp-kussmaul-sign]]
sections.title: Physical examination

sections.body:
### Tamponade vs constriction vs restriction vs RV infarction

| Feature | Tamponade | Constrictive pericarditis | Restrictive cardiomyopathy | RV infarction |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| JVP | Raised, **absent y** | Raised, **steep y**, M/W | Raised, steep y | Raised |
| Kussmaul sign | Rare | **Common** | Common | Common |
| Pulsus paradoxus | **Common** | Uncommon (about a third) | Rare | Can occur |
| Extra sound | - (quiet sounds) | **Pericardial knock** | S3, S4 | RV S3/S4 |
| Apex | Impalpable | Impalpable or retracted | Palpable | - |
| Setting | Effusion, trauma, rupture, dissection | Post-TB, post-surgery, radiation | Amyloid, sarcoid, haemochromatosis | Inferior STEMI |
| Key test | Echo (collapse, respiratory variation) | Echo/CMR/CT, catheter (discordance) | Echo strain, CMR, biopsy | ECG V4R, echo |

### Infective endocarditis: the peripheral signs

| Sign | Description | Mechanism | Duke class |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Splinter haemorrhages** | Linear red-brown streaks under the nails | Capillary emboli or vasculitis; non-specific (trauma) | - |
| **Janeway lesions** | **Painless** macules on palms and soles | Septic micro-emboli | Vascular phenomenon |
| **Osler nodes** | **Painful**, tender nodules in the finger and toe pulps | Immune-complex vasculitis | Immunological phenomenon |
| **Roth spots** | Retinal haemorrhages with a pale centre | Immune-complex vasculitis | Immunological phenomenon |
| Conjunctival haemorrhages | Petechiae on the conjunctiva | Emboli | Vascular phenomenon |
| Glomerulonephritis | Haematuria | Immune complexes | Immunological phenomenon |
| Clubbing, splenomegaly | Subacute disease | Chronic infection | - |

Memory hook: **O**sler = **O**uch (painful); **J**aneway = painless.
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body: **Why the y descent tells them apart:** in tamponade the fluid compresses the heart throughout diastole, so the RV cannot fill early and the y descent disappears; the heart only "makes room" during systolic emptying (x descent preserved). In constriction early diastolic filling is unimpeded and rapid until the shell is reached, so the y descent is steep and the filling stops abruptly (dip and plateau). In constriction the shell also **isolates the heart from intrathoracic pressure**, so inspiration cannot increase right-heart filling (Kussmaul sign), while in tamponade intrathoracic pressure is still transmitted and the inspiratory RV filling pushes the septum into the LV (pulsus paradoxus).
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Kussmaul sign = constriction**, pulsus paradoxus = tamponade; each can occasionally appear in the other.
- **Beck triad** describes acute (surgical) tamponade; a large chronic effusion may have normal blood pressure.
- Constriction is often misdiagnosed as **liver cirrhosis** (ascites, hepatomegaly): look at the neck veins.
- An S3 is normal under about 40 years; in an older patient with dyspnoea it is strong evidence of LV dysfunction.
- **Roth spots are not specific** to endocarditis (leukaemia, severe anaemia, diabetes, hypertension).
- In the ESC 2023 Duke criteria, Janeway lesions are **vascular** and Osler nodes and Roth spots are **immunological** minor criteria.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds after chest trauma" -> tamponade (Beck triad).
- "Raised JVP, Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, ascites, previous TB" -> constrictive pericarditis.
- "Fever, new murmur, painful finger-pulp nodules" -> endocarditis (Osler nodes); "painless palmar macules" -> Janeway lesions.
- "S3, raised JVP, bibasal crackles, cool peripheries, narrow pulse pressure" -> cold and wet heart failure.
- "Inferior STEMI, hypotension, raised JVP, clear lungs" -> RV infarction.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **Beck triad**: hypotension, raised JVP, quiet heart sounds (acute tamponade).
- Tamponade: **pulsus paradoxus, absent y**; constriction: **steep y, Kussmaul sign, knock**.
- **Ewart sign** = large pericardial effusion.
- HF profiles: warm/cold (perfusion) x dry/wet (congestion).
- **Osler painful (immunological), Janeway painless (vascular), Roth retinal (immunological)**, splinters non-specific.

sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: Bedside signs of heart failure, tamponade, constriction and endocarditis

sections.body:
This guide decides two things for a slow heart rate: **what to do now** (atropine, pacing, chronotropes) if the patient is unstable, and **whether a permanent pacemaker is needed**, which depends on the rhythm (sinus node vs AV node vs infra-Hisian), symptoms, and reversible causes.

*Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.*
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
First stability, then rhythm. In sinus node disease, symptoms decide. In Mobitz II, high-grade or complete AV block that is not reversible, the block itself decides - pace regardless of symptoms.

[[figure:bradycardia-av-block-algorithm]]
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
**AV block: level and pacing**

| Block | Usual level | QRS / escape | Atropine | Permanent pacing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| First-degree (PR >200 ms) | AV node | Narrow | Responds | Only if symptoms clearly attributable (marked PR prolongation) |
| Mobitz I (Wenckebach) | AV node | Narrow | Responds | Only if symptomatic or infra-Hisian |
| Mobitz II | His-Purkinje | Often wide | Often no effect | Yes, regardless of symptoms (if not reversible) |
| 2:1 | Either | Narrow suggests node, wide suggests infra-His | Variable | Decide by level and symptoms |
| High-grade / third-degree | Node (narrow escape 40-60) or infra-His (wide escape 20-40) | Variable | Node-level may respond | Yes, regardless of symptoms (if not reversible) |
| Alternating BBB | Infra-His | Wide | - | Yes, with or without symptoms (ESC 2021) |
| Bifascicular block + syncope | Infra-His | Wide | - | If HV >=70 ms or induced infra-His block (ESC 2021) |
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body:
**Acute drugs and devices**

| Step | Dose / detail | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Atropine | 1 mg IV every 3-5 min, maximum 3 mg | AHA ACLS (2020 change from 0.5 mg; carried into 2025 materials) |
| Dopamine | 5-20 mcg/kg/min | AHA ACLS |
| Epinephrine | 2-10 mcg/min | AHA ACLS |
| Transcutaneous pacing | Bridge; confirm mechanical capture | ACC/AHA/HRS 2018 (may be considered) |
| Temporary transvenous pacing | Persistent unstable bradycardia refractory to drugs | ACC/AHA/HRS 2018 (reasonable) |
| Permanent pacing, acquired Mobitz II / high-grade / CHB not reversible | Regardless of symptoms | ACC/AHA/HRS 2018 COR 1; ESC 2021 indicated |
| CRT or His-bundle pacing instead of RV pacing | LVEF 36-50% with expected ventricular pacing >40% | ACC/AHA/HRS 2018 (reasonable) |

**Reversible causes to check first:** beta-blocker, non-DHP CCB, digoxin, antiarrhythmics, hyperkalaemia, acute inferior MI, hypothyroidism, hypothermia, sleep apnoea, Lyme carditis, raised intracranial pressure.
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: Bradycardia questions hinge on locating the block. Once you know whether it is the sinus node, the AV node, or the His-Purkinje system, the acute drug response and the pacing indication follow logically.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Relying on atropine in Mobitz II or wide-escape complete block** - the block is below the node; go to pacing.
- **Atropine after heart transplant** - denervated heart, may cause paradoxical block; use pacing or catecholamines.
- **Pacing asymptomatic sinus bradycardia, sleep pauses or athletes** - not indicated.
- **Not pacing asymptomatic complete heart block** - acquired, non-reversible CHB or Mobitz II needs a pacemaker regardless of symptoms.
- **Calling drug-associated AV block 'reversible'** too quickly - it often unmasks intrinsic disease.
- **Electrical capture without a pulse** on transcutaneous pacing.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- Inferior STEMI with complete heart block, narrow escape at 50 bpm -> AV-nodal, often transient; revascularize, atropine, temporary pacing if unstable.
- Anterior STEMI with new RBBB and Mobitz II -> infra-Hisian, high risk -> temporary pacing.
- Asymptomatic 70-year-old with incidental complete heart block, wide escape 35 bpm -> permanent pacemaker.
- Fit 25-year-old runner with HR 42 and Mobitz I at night -> reassurance.
- AF with a regular ventricular rate of 40 on digoxin -> complete heart block / digoxin toxicity.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **Unstable bradycardia:** atropine 1 mg (max 3 mg) -> pacing or dopamine/epinephrine.
- **Narrow QRS block is usually nodal and benign; wide QRS block is infra-Hisian and dangerous.**
- **SND:** symptoms decide (no rate threshold); **acquired Mobitz II/high-grade/CHB:** pace regardless of symptoms.
- Minimise RV pacing in reduced LVEF: CRT or conduction-system pacing.
- After inferior MI, many AV blocks recover - observe before a permanent device (ESC 2021: wait at least 5 days).

title: Decision guide: bradycardia and AV block

sections.body:
This guide follows the 2025 AHA adult cardiac arrest algorithm: **shockable or not**, what goes in every 2-minute cycle, when each drug is due, which reversible cause to hunt, and what to do after ROSC. ERC differences in drug timing are flagged.

*Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.*
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
[[figure:cardiac-arrest-algorithm]]

**CPR quality**: rate 100-120/min; depth at least 5 cm but not more than 6 cm; full recoil; pauses under 10 s; 30:2 until an advanced airway, then 1 breath every 6 s with continuous compressions; avoid over-ventilation; change compressor every 2 min; single shocks (not stacked), CPR resumed immediately after each shock. Vascular access: **IV first** (AHA 2025 COR 1, A), IO if IV fails (2a A).
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
### Arrest drugs and timing
| Drug | Dose | When (AHA) | Class (AHA 2025) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Adrenaline (epinephrine) | 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 min | Non-shockable: as soon as feasible. Shockable: after initial shocks fail (usually after shock 2) | 2a B-R (dose); 2a B-NR (timing) |
| Amiodarone | 300 mg bolus, then 150 mg | Persisting VF/pVT (after shock 3) | 2b B-R (amiodarone or lidocaine) |
| Lidocaine | 1-1.5 mg/kg, then 0.5-0.75 mg/kg | Alternative to amiodarone | 2b B-R |
| Vasopressin | - | Do not substitute for adrenaline | 3: No Benefit |
| High-dose adrenaline | - | Not routine | 3: No Benefit |
| Calcium, bicarbonate, magnesium | - | Not routine; only for specific causes (hyperkalaemia, toxins, torsades) | 3: No Benefit (routine use) |
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body:
### Post-ROSC targets (AHA 2025)
| Item | Target | Class |
|---|---|---|
| Mean arterial pressure | ≥65 mmHg | 1, B-R |
| Oxygen | 100% until reliable SpO2, then SpO2 90-98% (PaO2 60-105) | 1 / 2a, B-R |
| PaCO2 | 35-45 mmHg | 1, B-R |
| Temperature (not following commands) | 32-37.5 °C | 1, B-R |
| Duration of temperature control | At least 36 h | 2a, B-R |
| Coronary angiography: ST elevation | Emergent | 1, B-NR |
| Coronary angiography: no STE, stable | Not emergent | 3: No Benefit, B-R |
| Prognostication | Multimodal, ≥72 h after normothermia | 2a, B-NR |

**H's and T's**: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo-/hyperkalaemia, hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis (pulmonary), thrombosis (coronary).
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: Every cardiology resident leads resuscitations from the first week. The exam tests the sequence and the timing rather than rare facts, and post-ROSC care (angiography, temperature, targets) is where cardiologists make the decisions that change neurological outcome.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- Giving adrenaline **before the first shock** in VF: defibrillation comes first; adrenaline after initial shocks fail.
- Delaying adrenaline in asystole/PEA (give it as soon as feasible).
- Stacked shocks or long pauses for pulse checks.
- Atropine in asystole/PEA (removed from the arrest algorithm since 2010).
- Routine calcium, bicarbonate or magnesium (no benefit; reserve for specific causes).
- Emergency angiography for every comatose survivor without ST elevation (no benefit if stable).
- Prognosticating on day 1: wait at least 72 h after normothermia, off sedation, multimodal.
- Using ETCO2 alone to stop resuscitation.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- 'Drug after the 2nd shock in VF?' -> **adrenaline 1 mg** (AHA). 'After the 3rd shock?' -> **amiodarone 300 mg**.
- ERC: both adrenaline and amiodarone after the **3rd** shock.
- Arrest in a dialysis patient with peaked T waves -> **calcium** + treat hyperkalaemia.
- PEA arrest after a long flight, dilated RV on POCUS -> **thrombolysis** for PE.
- Sudden ETCO2 jump from 15 to 40 mmHg during CPR -> **ROSC**.
- Comatose after ROSC: temperature control 32-37.5 °C for ≥36 h; MAP ≥65.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Shockable: shock -> CPR 2 min -> repeat; adrenaline after shock 2, amiodarone after shock 3 (AHA).
- Non-shockable: adrenaline ASAP, every 3-5 min.
- Amiodarone 300 then 150; lidocaine 1-1.5 then 0.5-0.75 mg/kg.
- DSED/vector change: not established (2b).
- Post-ROSC: MAP ≥65; SpO2 90-98%; PaCO2 35-45; 32-37.5 °C ≥36 h; prognosis ≥72 h.

sections.body:
**Cardiogenic shock** is a cardiac disorder causing clinical and biochemical evidence of sustained tissue hypoperfusion; hypotension is usual but not required (normotensive shock). This guide stages severity (SCAI), finds the cause, and picks the right reperfusion, device and drug.

*Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.*
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
[[figure:cardiogenic-shock-algorithm]]

- Every suspected shock: **ECG, lactate, bedside echo** within minutes.
- Phenotype (PA catheter if available): LV-dominant (PCWP >15), RV-dominant (RA/CVP >15 with normal PCWP; RA:PCWP >0.6), or biventricular.
- Cardiac power output and PAPi (AMI-CS: <0.9) help choose and escalate support.
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
### SCAI SHOCK stages (2019, updated 2022)
| Stage | Description | Typical findings |
|---|---|---|
| A - At risk | No shock yet | Normal JVP, warm, lactate normal, SBP ≥100 or baseline |
| B - Beginning | Instability without hypoperfusion | SBP <90, MAP <60 or drop >30 mmHg, or HR ≥100; lactate normal; perfusion intact |
| C - Classic | Hypoperfusion needing one intervention beyond fluids | Cold/clammy, oliguria, confusion; lactate ≥2; CI <2.2, PCWP >15 |
| D - Deteriorating | Like C but worsening despite initial therapy | Rising lactate, worsening organ function, escalating drugs or MCS |
| E - Extremis | Circulatory collapse | Ongoing CPR/ECMO; lactate ≥8, pH <7.2, base deficit >10 |
| Modifier 'A' | Cardiac arrest with coma | GCS <9 after arrest; worse prognosis at any stage |
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body:
- **Emergency culprit revascularisation** (PCI or CABG) in ACS-CS irrespective of time from onset: ACC/AHA 2025 COR 1 B-R; ESC 2023 Class I.
- **No routine multivessel PCI** in shock: ACC/AHA 2025 3: Harm B-R.
- **Microaxial flow pump** in selected STEMI-CS: ACC/AHA 2025 2a B-R.
- **Routine IABP or VA-ECMO**: ACC/AHA 2025 3: No Benefit B-R; ESC 2023 routine IABP III.
- **Norepinephrine** first vasopressor; inotrope for low output; avoid dopamine.
- Treat shock in a hub centre with a **shock team** (interventional, HF, critical care, cardiac surgery).

### Mechanical complications of MI
| Complication | Clue | Echo | Treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ventricular septal rupture | New harsh holosystolic murmur, thrill, biventricular failure | Shunt across the septum; O2 step-up RA -> RV | Surgery (or selected transcatheter closure); MCS/IABP bridge |
| Papillary muscle rupture | Sudden pulmonary oedema; murmur soft or absent | Flail leaflet, severe MR, hyperdynamic LV | Emergency mitral surgery; afterload reduction, MCS bridge |
| Free-wall rupture | Sudden PEA/tamponade | Effusion with tamponade, pseudoaneurysm | Emergency surgery |
| RV infarction | Inferior STEMI, V4R ST elevation, raised JVP, clear lungs | Dilated hypokinetic RV | Preload, avoid nitrates, pacing, reperfusion |
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: Cardiogenic shock still kills about 40-50% of patients with MI-related shock. The exam rewards a structured approach: stage it, find a fixable cause, open the culprit artery, and know which trials killed routine IABP, routine ECMO and multivessel PCI.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- Waiting for hypotension: **normotensive shock** with rising lactate is already stage C.
- Multivessel PCI at the index procedure in shock (CULPRIT-SHOCK: more death or renal replacement therapy).
- Routine IABP (IABP-SHOCK II) or routine ECMO (ECLS-SHOCK): no survival benefit.
- Dopamine as the first vasopressor.
- Nitrates or diuretics in RV infarction.
- Missing a **soft** murmur in papillary muscle rupture (the louder murmur is VSR).
- Needle drainage of haemopericardium from aortic dissection or free-wall rupture instead of surgery.
- Adding drug after drug in stage D instead of rethinking the cause and calling the shock team.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- Day 3 after inferior MI, sudden pulmonary oedema, hyperdynamic LV, soft murmur -> **posteromedial papillary muscle rupture**.
- Day 4 after anterior MI, new loud holosystolic murmur with thrill, O2 step-up -> **VSR**.
- Inferior STEMI, hypotension after GTN, clear lungs, raised JVP -> **RV infarct**: fluids, not nitrates.
- STEMI with shock 20 hours after onset -> still **emergency PCI** (time limit does not apply in shock).
- 'Vasopressor of choice in cardiogenic shock?' -> **norepinephrine**.
- SCAI stage with lactate 9 and ongoing CPR -> **E**.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- SCAI A-E; B = instability without hypoperfusion; C = hypoperfusion + 1 intervention.
- Lactate ≥2 = hypoperfusion; ≥8 = extremis.
- Culprit-only PCI, any time from onset.
- DanGer-Shock: microaxial pump reduced death in selected STEMI-CS (cost: bleeding, limb ischaemia).
- Norepinephrine first; dobutamine/milrinone for low output.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

sections.body:
This page covers the echo signatures examiners expect you to recognise in one glance: **hypertrophic** (HCM, with or without obstruction), **dilated**, **restrictive/infiltrative** (amyloidosis) and **stress (Takotsubo)** cardiomyopathy; **pericardial effusion, tamponade and constriction**; and **masses** (vegetation, thrombus, tumour) with the indications for transoesophageal echo (TOE).

**Guideline currency:** the pericardial content follows the ESC 2015 pericardial diseases guideline. The ESC 2025 guideline on myocarditis and pericarditis has since replaced it and may change the effusion and tamponade statements quoted here; verify against the 2025 text.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
**HCM** (ESC 2023): LV wall thickness **15 mm or more** in any segment (13 mm or more in a relative or a genotype-positive person) not explained by loading. Usually asymmetric septal; variants include apical HCM ("ace of spades" cavity). Look for **systolic anterior motion (SAM)** of the mitral valve, a posteriorly directed mid-to-late systolic MR jet, mid-systolic aortic valve closure on M-mode, and an LVOT gradient.

[[figure:echo-hocm-dagger-cw]]

**LVOT obstruction** = peak gradient **30 mmHg or more** at rest or with provocation (Valsalva, standing, exercise echo); **50 mmHg or more** is haemodynamically important and the threshold for septal reduction therapy when symptoms persist on medical therapy.

**DCM**: dilated, spherical LV with global hypokinesia, increased EPSS, functional MR, sometimes apical thrombus (see "LV size and systolic function").

**Cardiac amyloidosis**: thick LV walls with **low ECG voltage**, thick valves and interatrial septum, biatrial enlargement, small effusion, restrictive filling with very low e', and **apical sparing** of longitudinal strain (a "cherry-on-top" bull's-eye).

**Takotsubo**: apical (or mid-ventricular, basal) ballooning with a hyperkinetic base; the wall-motion abnormality **extends beyond one coronary territory**; possible LVOT obstruction from basal hypercontraction (avoid inotropes); recovery within days to weeks.

[[figure:echo-tamponade-respiratory-variation]]

**Pericardial effusion** size at end-diastole (ESC 2015; check ESC 2025): small under 10 mm, moderate 10-20 mm, large over 20 mm. **Tamponade** is a clinical diagnosis supported by echo: RA systolic collapse (lasting more than a third of the cycle is more specific), RV early diastolic collapse (more specific), a **plethoric IVC** without inspiratory collapse (most sensitive), and **exaggerated reciprocal respiratory variation** of inflow (mitral E falls with inspiration by more than about 25-30%, tricuspid E rises by more than about 40-60%).
sections.title: Echocardiography

sections.body:
**Constriction vs restriction** (both: small or normal LV, normal LVEF, raised filling pressures, restrictive-looking inflow):

| Feature | Constrictive pericarditis | Restrictive cardiomyopathy |
|---|---|---|
| Septum | respiratory shift, septal bounce | normal motion |
| Mitral E respiratory variation | over 25% | small |
| Medial e' | preserved or high (annulus paradoxus) | reduced |
| Lateral vs medial e' | lateral lower than medial (annulus reversus) | normal relation (lateral higher) |
| Hepatic vein | expiratory diastolic flow reversal | inspiratory diastolic flow reversal |
| Atria, PA pressure | mild atrial enlargement, PASP usually under 50 mmHg | marked biatrial enlargement, PASP often over 50 mmHg |
| Pericardium | thickened or calcified (CT, CMR) | normal |

**Masses:**

| Mass | Typical site | Clue |
|---|---|---|
| Myxoma | LA, stalk on the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis | mobile, may prolapse into the mitral orifice in diastole |
| Thrombus | LV apex after anterior MI; LAA in AF or MS | next to an akinetic segment; LAA needs TOE; contrast helps at the apex |
| Papillary fibroelastoma | valves (aortic most often), usually downstream side | small, mobile, frond-like, embolic |
| Vegetation | upstream (low-pressure) side: atrial side of AV valves, ventricular side of aortic valve | irregular, oscillating, with regurgitation, abscess or fistula |
| Normal variants | Chiari network, Eustachian valve, crista terminalis (RA); moderator band; false tendon; coumadin ridge (LAA-LUPV) | not pathology |

**Endocarditis (ESC 2023)**: TTE first; **TOE** when TTE is negative or non-diagnostic with ongoing suspicion, with a prosthetic valve or intracardiac device, and in practically every patient with suspected IE even when TTE is positive (except isolated right-sided native-valve IE with good-quality TTE), to detect complications (abscess, pseudoaneurysm, fistula, perforation) and before surgery; repeat TTE/TOE within 5-7 days if the first study is negative and suspicion persists.
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
- **Athlete's heart vs HCM**: athletes have a dilated LV cavity (often over 55 mm), normal e', symmetric wall usually 16 mm or less, and regression with deconditioning.
- Missing **latent obstruction**: always provoke (Valsalva, standing, exercise) when the resting gradient is under 30 mmHg.
- Treating Takotsubo with LVOT obstruction with **inotropes or nitrates**.
- Calling **epicardial fat** an effusion, or a **pleural** effusion pericardial (descending aorta landmark).
- Expecting RV collapse in tamponade with **pulmonary hypertension or RV hypertrophy** (it may be absent); loculated post-surgical effusions can compress only one chamber.
- Using **E/e'** to estimate pressure in constriction (paradoxically low).
- Taking a negative TTE as excluding endocarditis, especially with a prosthetic valve.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Septum 22 mm, SAM, late-peaking dagger 4.2 m/s rising with Valsalva" = obstructive HCM.
- "Thick walls, low voltage ECG, apical sparing strain, biatrial enlargement" = cardiac amyloidosis.
- "Postmenopausal woman after emotional stress, apical ballooning, non-obstructed coronaries" = Takotsubo.
- "Hypotension, large effusion, RV diastolic collapse, plethoric IVC, mitral E falls 35% with inspiration" = tamponade: pericardiocentesis.
- "Septal bounce, medial e' 12 cm/s, expiratory hepatic vein reversal" = constrictive pericarditis.
- "Pedunculated LA mass attached to the fossa ovalis" = myxoma.
- "Prosthetic valve, fever, negative TTE" = TOE.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- HCM: wall 15 mm or more (13 mm in relatives); LVOT obstruction 30 mmHg or more, 50 mmHg or more for septal reduction.
- Amyloid: thick walls + low voltage + apical sparing strain + restrictive filling.
- Takotsubo: wall-motion abnormality beyond one coronary territory with a hyperkinetic base.
- Effusion: small under 10 mm, moderate 10-20 mm, large over 20 mm; RV diastolic collapse is the most specific chamber sign, a plethoric IVC the most sensitive.
- Constriction: annulus paradoxus and reversus, septal bounce, expiratory hepatic vein reversal.
- TOE for prosthetic valves, devices, a negative TTE with ongoing suspicion, a positive TTE (except isolated right-sided native-valve IE) and complications.

Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

title: Cardiomyopathies, pericardium and masses: HCM, DCM, amyloid, Takotsubo, tamponade, endocarditis

sections.body:
This guide walks one decision: a patient with possible ACS arrives - **which pathway, and how fast?** The first ECG (within 10 minutes of first medical contact) splits patients into STEMI (or a STEMI equivalent) and NSTE-ACS; troponin and risk then set the timing of angiography. Shock overrides everything.

*Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.*
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
Use the tree in order: **instability first, ECG second, time third, troponin and risk last.** Reperfusion in STEMI is never delayed for a troponin result.

[[figure:chest-pain-acs-algorithm]]

ESC 2023 and ACC/AHA 2025 agree on the architecture. The main difference is the clock: ACC/AHA counts from **first medical contact** (device <=90 min, <=120 min with transfer); ESC counts **120 min from STEMI diagnosis** when choosing PPCI over fibrinolysis, and ESC 2023 considers routine primary PCI up to 48 h after onset (IIa, B).
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
**Numbers and classes to know**

| Decision | ACC/AHA 2025 | ESC 2023 |
|---|---|---|
| ECG after first contact | Within 10 min (COR 1, B-NR) | Within 10 min |
| PPCI, STEMI <12 h | FMC-to-device <=90 min, <=120 min if transferred (COR 1, A) | PPCI if <120 min from diagnosis |
| Fibrinolysis | <12 h and expected PPCI delay >120 min, no contraindication (COR 1, A) | When PPCI not possible within 120 min of diagnosis |
| After fibrinolysis | Immediate transfer (1, A); angiography 2-24 h (1, B-R); rescue PCI if failed (1, B-R) | Angiography 2-24 h (I, A); rescue PCI if failed (I, A) |
| STEMI 12-24 h | PPCI reasonable (2a, B-NR) | Routine PPCI 12-48 h should be considered (IIa, B) |
| Stable, occluded artery >24 h | No PPCI (3: No benefit, B-R) | No routine PCI of an occluded IRA >48 h if asymptomatic (III, A) |
| ST depression only | No fibrinolysis (3: Harm, B-R) unless posterior STEMI | Same principle |
| NSTE-ACS, refractory angina or instability | Immediate invasive <2 h (1, C-LD) | Immediate <2 h (very high risk; I, C) |
| NSTE-ACS, high risk | Early invasive <24 h (2a, B-R) | Early <24 h should be considered (IIa, A) |
| hs-cTn repeat sample | 1-2 h (conventional cTn 3-6 h) (1, B-NR) | 0h/1h best, 0h/2h second best |
| ACS with shock | Culprit-vessel revascularization regardless of time (1, B-R); no routine non-culprit PCI (3: Harm, B-R) | Immediate invasive |
| Resuscitated arrest, comatose, stable, no STEMI | Immediate angiography not recommended (3: No benefit, A) | No routine immediate angiography (III, A) |
| MCS in STEMI shock | Microaxial pump in selected (2a, B-R); routine IABP/VA-ECMO no (3: No benefit, B-R) | - |

**STEMI ECG criteria** (ACC/AHA 2025 Table 3, from the 4th UDMI)

| Leads | ST elevation at J point, 2 contiguous leads |
|---|---|
| All leads except V2-V3 | >=1 mm |
| V2-V3, men >=40 y | >=2 mm |
| V2-V3, men <40 y | >=2.5 mm |
| V2-V3, women | >=1.5 mm |
| V7-V9 (posterior) | >=0.5 mm (>=1 mm in men <40 y) |

**Failed fibrinolysis** = <50% ST resolution in anterior leads or <70% in inferior leads, ongoing pain, or instability (ACC/AHA 2025 Sec 5.3.2).
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body:
**ESC 2023 NSTE-ACS risk groups**

| Group | Criteria (any one) | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Very high risk | Haemodynamic instability or cardiogenic shock; recurrent/refractory pain despite treatment; life-threatening arrhythmia; mechanical complication; ACS-related acute HF; recurrent dynamic ST/T changes | Immediate (<2 h) |
| High risk | NSTEMI confirmed by hs-cTn algorithm; dynamic ST/T changes; transient ST elevation; GRACE >140 | Early (<24 h) |
| Not high risk | None of the above | Selective invasive after non-invasive testing (ESC); invasive before discharge reasonable for intermediate risk (ACC/AHA) |
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: Most ACS exam questions are really timing questions. If you can say, for any vignette, which pathway the patient is on and which clock is running, the drug and device details fall into place.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Waiting for troponin in STEMI.** Reperfusion is decided on the ECG; troponin never delays it.
- **Fibrinolysis for ST depression.** It is harmful (COR 3: Harm) unless true posterior STEMI is suspected - record V7-V9 first.
- **New LBBB = STEMI.** Not on its own: ACC/AHA 2025 says new LBBB is not diagnostic in isolation and is not a STEMI equivalent when asymptomatic; it matters with ongoing ischaemic symptoms or instability.
- **Multivessel PCI in shock.** Culprit-only at the index procedure (CULPRIT-SHOCK); non-culprit PCI in shock is harmful.
- **Routine IABP in shock.** No survival benefit (IABP-SHOCK II); the microaxial pump is 2a only in *selected* STEMI shock and has more bleeding and limb ischaemia.
- **Mixing the clocks.** ACC/AHA's 90/120 min are from first medical contact; ESC's 120 min decision is from diagnosis.
- **Opening a stable occluded artery after 24-48 h** - no benefit (OAT).
- **Immediate angiography for every resuscitated arrest.** Comatose, electrically and haemodynamically stable, no STEMI: not recommended (ACC/AHA 2025 3: No benefit, A; ESC 2023 III A). With STEMI on the ECG: PPCI.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- Rural hospital without a cath lab, transfer >2 h, symptoms 3 h, no contraindication -> **fibrinolysis then transfer, angiography 2-24 h** (pharmaco-invasive). Very relevant to Indonesian regional hospitals.
- Inferior STEMI + hypotension + clear lungs -> right-sided leads (V4R), think RV infarction: fluids, avoid nitrates.
- ST depression V1-V3 with tall R in V1-V2 -> posterior MI -> V7-V9.
- 60 min after lysis, pain persists and ST resolution 30% -> **rescue PCI**.
- NSTEMI with recurrent pain and VT on medical therapy -> immediate (<2 h) angiography.
- NSTEMI, pain-free, GRACE 150 -> angiography within 24 h.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **Three clocks:** ECG <=10 min; FMC-to-device <=90 min (<=120 min with transfer); angiography 2-24 h after lysis.
- **PPCI beats lysis when timely**; each 30-min PPCI delay raises 1-year mortality ~7.5% (relative).
- **NSTE-ACS timing ladder:** immediate <2 h (very high risk) -> early <24 h (high risk) -> before discharge / selective (others).
- **hs-cTn:** rise and/or fall with >=1 value >99th percentile URL; repeat at 1-2 h; assay-specific thresholds; single-sample rule-out only >=3 h after onset.
- **Fifth Universal Definition of MI (ESC/ACC/AHA/WHF 2026)** replaces numbered types with clinical categories: primary (formerly type 1), secondary (formerly type 2) and procedure-related MI (formerly types 4 and 5; type 3 is no longer a separate category), with sex-specific 99th-percentile troponin limits; MINOCA's 'I' now means 'injury' as a working diagnosis.
- PERKI's ACS guidance generally follows ESC; check the current PERKI edition for local adaptations (not verified here).

title: Decision guide: chest pain and suspected ACS (STEMI vs NSTE-ACS)

sections.body:
**Diastolic dysfunction** is impaired LV relaxation and/or increased chamber stiffness. Echo does two jobs: decide whether diastolic function is **normal**, and estimate whether the **mean left atrial pressure (LV filling pressure) is raised** - the cause of breathlessness in HFpEF and of congestion in HFrEF.

The ASE/EACVI 2016 recommendations replaced older multi-parameter schemes with two simple algorithms built on four variables: **annular e'**, **average E/e'**, **peak TR velocity** and **LA volume index**, with the **mitral inflow (E/A, E)** used for grading.

**Guideline currency:** this page teaches the ASE/EACVI 2016 algorithms, which most exam material still uses. ASE published an updated recommendation on diastolic function and HFpEF diagnosis in 2025 (Nagueh et al., JASE 2025); it revises the algorithms and may change the criteria, cut-offs and supplementary parameters given here. Check which version your examination expects and verify against the 2025 text.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
- **E wave** = early filling, driven by the LA-LV gradient: it rises with LA pressure and falls with slow relaxation.
- **A wave** = atrial contraction: it is large when early filling is poor (impaired relaxation) and small when the LV is stiff and the LA pressure high (restrictive) or when the atrium fails.
- **e'** (tissue Doppler of the mitral annulus) reflects relaxation and is relatively **preload-independent**, so **E/e'** tracks filling pressure.
- A chronically raised LA pressure enlarges the LA (**LAVI**, the "HbA1c" of filling pressure) and raises pulmonary pressure (**TR velocity**).
- With ageing, relaxation slows: E/A falls under 1 and e' falls; this alone is not disease.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body:
[[figure:echo-mitral-inflow-normal]]

[[figure:echo-tissue-doppler-septal]]

**How to measure:** mitral inflow with PW at the **leaflet tips** (A4C); e' with tissue Doppler at the **septal and lateral annulus** (average them); TR velocity with CW from several windows; LA volume by biplane disc summation at end-systole, indexed to body surface area.

[[figure:echo-mitral-inflow-impaired-relaxation]]

[[figure:echo-mitral-inflow-pseudonormal]]

[[figure:echo-mitral-inflow-restrictive]]

The **pseudonormal** pattern looks normal (E larger than A) because a raised LA pressure restores the early gradient. It is unmasked by a low e', a high E/e', a large LA, a raised TR velocity, or a fall in E/A of 50% or more during **Valsalva** (preload reduction).
sections.title: Echocardiography

sections.body:
[[figure:echo-diastolic-function-algorithm]]

1. **Can the algorithm be used?** Atrial fibrillation, significant mitral valve disease, mitral annular calcification, prosthetic mitral valves, heart transplant and LVAD need specific approaches.
2. **Choose the algorithm** by LVEF and the presence of myocardial disease (LVH, HCM, infiltration, regional wall-motion abnormality).
3. **Count criteria, do not cherry-pick**: one abnormal E/e' does not make HFpEF.
4. **Grade with the inflow** and report the LA pressure (normal, raised or indeterminate).
5. **Supplementary signs** when indeterminate: pulmonary vein flow (S/D under 1 and atrial reversal Ar duration more than 30 ms longer than mitral A = raised LV end-diastolic pressure), an L wave (mid-diastolic flow), LA strain, and **diastolic stress echo** (positive when, with exercise, average E/e' is over 14 or septal E/e' over 15, peak TR velocity over 2.8 m/s and septal e' under 7 cm/s).
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
**Abnormal values (ASE/EACVI 2016):** average E/e' over 14; septal e' under 7 cm/s or lateral e' under 10 cm/s; peak TR velocity over 2.8 m/s; LA volume index over 34 mL/m2.

**Algorithm 1 (normal LVEF, no myocardial disease):** 0-1 of 4 abnormal = normal diastolic function; 2 of 4 = indeterminate; 3-4 of 4 = diastolic dysfunction (grade it with algorithm 2).

**Algorithm 2 (reduced LVEF, or myocardial disease with normal LVEF): grading (ASE/EACVI 2016)**

| | Normal | Grade I | Grade II | Grade III |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| LV relaxation | normal | impaired | impaired | impaired |
| Mean LA pressure | normal | low or normal | raised | raised |
| Mitral E/A | 0.8 or more | 0.8 or less | over 0.8 to under 2 | 2 or more |
| Average E/e' | under 10 | under 10 | 10-14 | over 14 |
| Peak TR velocity | under 2.8 m/s | under 2.8 m/s | over 2.8 m/s | over 2.8 m/s |
| LA volume index | normal | normal or increased | increased | increased |

Grading rules: E/A 0.8 or less with E 50 cm/s or less = grade I (normal LA pressure); E/A 2 or more = grade III; otherwise **two of the three** criteria (E/e' over 14, TR over 2.8 m/s, LAVI over 34 mL/m2) decide: 2-3 positive = grade II, 2-3 negative = grade I, only one criterion available, or two available and they disagree = indeterminate.
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body:
- Calling **E/A under 1 in a 75-year-old** "diastolic dysfunction" when e', E/e', TR velocity and LAVI are normal.
- Missing the **pseudonormal** pattern by reading the inflow alone.
- Using **lateral e' cut-offs for the septum** (septal is normally lower: abnormal under 7 vs under 10 cm/s).
- Sampling inflow at the **annulus** instead of the leaflet tips (lower E, wrong DT).
- Applying E/e' in **constrictive pericarditis**: e' is preserved or high (annulus paradoxus), so E/e' underestimates the pressure.
- Grading diastolic function in **AF** with E/A (there is no A wave).
- A large LA in an **athlete** or with **mitral disease** or **AF** is not by itself evidence of raised pressure.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "E/A 0.6, DT 260 ms, E 45 cm/s" = grade I, normal LA pressure.
- "E/A 1.4, septal e' 5 cm/s, E/e' 17, LAVI 40 mL/m2" = grade II (pseudonormal), raised LA pressure.
- "E/A 2.8, DT 130 ms" = grade III restrictive; seen in decompensated HFrEF and amyloidosis.
- "E/A falls from 1.4 to 0.6 with Valsalva" = pseudonormal unmasked.
- "Normal LVEF, 2 of 4 criteria abnormal" = indeterminate.
- "HFpEF suspected, normal resting indices" = diastolic stress echo or invasive haemodynamics.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Four numbers: **E/e' over 14, septal e' under 7 / lateral e' under 10 cm/s, TR over 2.8 m/s, LAVI over 34 mL/m2**.
- Normal LVEF: more than half normal = normal; half = indeterminate; more than half abnormal = dysfunction.
- Grade I: E/A 0.8 or less and E 50 cm/s or less; grade III: E/A 2 or more; in between, 2 of 3 criteria decide.
- e' reflects relaxation and is relatively preload-independent; E/e' estimates LA pressure.
- Valsalva: a fall of E/A of 50% or more suggests raised filling pressure.

title: Diastolic function and filling pressures: E/A, e', E/e', LA volume and TR velocity (ASE/EACVI 2016)

sections.body: Doppler echocardiography measures the **velocity of moving blood or tissue** from the frequency shift of reflected ultrasound. Every haemodynamic number on an echo report - gradients, valve areas, stroke volume, pulmonary pressure, filling pressure - comes from a handful of equations. Knowing their **assumptions** is how exam questions about "discrepant" results are solved. The derivations are on the Physiology II page **"Valve hemodynamics: gradients, continuity equation and orifice area"**.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
- **Doppler equation**: frequency shift = 2 x f0 x v x cos(theta) / c (c = 1540 m/s). An intercept angle of 20 degrees underestimates velocity by about 6%, 60 degrees by 50%: **misalignment always underestimates**.
- **Simplified Bernoulli**: pressure gradient (mmHg) = 4 x v squared (m/s). Include the proximal velocity, 4 x (v2 squared - v1 squared), when it is high (LVOT velocity over about 1.5 m/s, or AS velocity under 3 m/s).
- **Continuity**: flow is conserved, A1 x VTI1 = A2 x VTI2, so AVA = LVOT area x VTI(LVOT) / VTI(AV).
- **PISA**: flow = 2 x pi x r squared x aliasing velocity; EROA = flow / peak regurgitant velocity.
- **Qp/Qs** = (RVOT area x RVOT VTI) / (LVOT area x LVOT VTI); 1.5 or more suggests a significant left-to-right shunt.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body:
[[figure:echo-lvot-pw-vti]]

| Mode | Strength | Limitation | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pulsed-wave (PW) | velocity at one depth (range resolution) | aliases above the Nyquist limit (PRF / 2) | LVOT VTI, mitral inflow, pulmonary veins, RVOT |
| Continuous-wave (CW) | measures high velocities, no aliasing | no depth information (range ambiguity) | AS, MR, TR, AR, HCM gradients |
| Colour Doppler | map of flow direction and turbulence | aliasing, gain- and Nyquist-dependent jet size | regurgitant jets, shunts, PISA, vena contracta |
| Tissue Doppler | low-velocity, high-amplitude myocardial signal | angle-dependent | e', s', a', TAPSE complement |
| Speckle-tracking strain | angle-independent deformation | vendor-dependent values | GLS, RV strain, LA strain |

**Aliasing** (PW or colour): the velocity exceeds the Nyquist limit and wraps around. Fix by moving the baseline, raising the PRF (velocity scale; a shallower sample depth allows a higher PRF), using a lower transducer frequency, or switching to CW.

[[figure:echo-tr-cw-pulmonary-hypertension]]

**Pressures from velocities:**

| Estimate | Formula |
|---|---|
| RV (PA) systolic pressure | 4 x TR peak velocity squared + RAP |
| PA diastolic pressure | 4 x PR end-diastolic velocity squared + RAP |
| Mean PA pressure | 4 x PR early-diastolic peak velocity squared + RAP (approximately) |
| LA systolic pressure | systolic BP - 4 x MR peak velocity squared (no AS or LVOT obstruction) |
| LV end-diastolic pressure | diastolic BP - 4 x AR end-diastolic velocity squared |
sections.title: Echocardiography

sections.body:
When Doppler and catheter (or two echo measures) disagree, ask which assumption failed:

1. **Angle**: Doppler underestimates; look for the highest velocity in several windows.
2. **Peak instantaneous vs peak-to-peak**: the Doppler peak gradient (instantaneous) is higher than the catheter peak-to-peak gradient, which is not a physiological instant; **mean gradients** agree best.
3. **Pressure recovery**: in a small ascending aorta (under 3 cm) part of the pressure lost at the vena contracta is recovered downstream, so Doppler overestimates the net gradient (also with bileaflet mechanical valves).
4. **Flow**: gradients depend on flow; low flow lowers them (low-flow AS), high flow raises them (anaemia, AR, pregnancy, sepsis).
5. **LVOT diameter**: squared in every area; DVI avoids it.
6. **Wrong jet**: the MR jet near the LVOT is faster and longer (starts at mitral closure); the HCM jet is late-peaking.
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
- Believing a CW velocity can be **overestimated by angle**: it cannot (except by recording the wrong jet).
- Ignoring the proximal velocity when the LVOT velocity is high (subvalvular plus valvular obstruction, AR with high flow).
- Grading regurgitation by **colour jet area**: depends on gain, Nyquist limit, driving pressure, and eccentric jets hug the wall (Coanda effect).
- Using **PW** for a jet above its Nyquist limit (aliased peak).
- Sampling the LVOT VTI too close to the valve (flow acceleration overestimates it) or in the wrong place.
- Forgetting heart rate when comparing gradients and VTIs, and averaging several beats in AF.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Catheter peak-to-peak 50 mmHg, Doppler peak 70 mmHg" = expected difference (instantaneous vs peak-to-peak); compare means.
- "Moderate AS, ascending aorta 2.6 cm, Doppler gradient higher than catheter" = pressure recovery.
- "PW peak cut off and wrapped below the baseline" = aliasing: switch to CW or raise the PRF.
- "TR 3.0 m/s, RAP 15 mmHg" = RVSP 51 mmHg.
- "LVOT diameter 2.0 cm, VTI 20 cm" = SV about 63 mL.
- "Qp/Qs 2.0" = large left-to-right shunt.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Gradient = 4v squared; misalignment always underestimates; 20 degrees = about 6% error.
- Nyquist limit = PRF / 2: PW aliases, CW does not (but has no depth resolution).
- Continuity: AVA = LVOT area x VTI(LVOT) / VTI(AV); SV = 0.785 x D squared x VTI.
- PISA: EROA = 2 pi r squared x Va / Vmax.
- Doppler peak instantaneous gradient exceeds catheter peak-to-peak; pressure recovery in a small aorta.
- RVSP = 4 TRV squared + RAP; LAP = SBP - 4 MR velocity squared (no AS or LVOT obstruction).

Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

sections.body: **Dynamic auscultation** changes preload, afterload, heart rate or right-heart filling for a few beats and listens to what the murmur does. Two lesions behave "the wrong way" and are the reason the exam asks about manoeuvres: the murmur of **obstructive HCM** and the click and murmur of **mitral valve prolapse** both get **louder (and MVP earlier and longer) when the left ventricle gets smaller**. Almost every other murmur gets softer when preload falls. The mechanism of each manoeuvre is introduced on the Physiology II page **"Heart sounds and murmurs: the physiology"**; this page is the lesion-by-lesion table and the reasoning behind it.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
### What each manoeuvre does

- **Inspiration**: lower intrathoracic pressure, more venous return to the **right** heart -> right-sided murmurs and sounds increase (**Carvallo sign** for TR); left-sided ones change little or soften slightly.
- **Valsalva strain (phase II)**: forced expiration against a closed glottis for about 10-15 s raises intrathoracic pressure, **venous return and LV size fall**, stroke volume falls. On release, right-sided murmurs return to baseline within about 2-3 beats, left-sided ones only after about 5-10 beats.
- **Standing (from squatting or lying)**: blood pools in the legs, **preload falls** (similar to Valsalva).
- **Squatting**: venous return rises (**more preload**) and kinking of the leg arteries raises **afterload**; the LV gets bigger.
- **Passive leg raise**: **more preload** only (no afterload change).
- **Sustained isometric handgrip** (about 1 minute): **more afterload** (systemic resistance and BP rise), with some rise in heart rate and cardiac output.
- **Transient arterial occlusion** (cuffs on both arms inflated above systolic for 20 s): more afterload, like handgrip.
- **Amyl nitrite inhalation**: potent arterial vasodilator: **afterload falls** sharply, then reflex tachycardia and higher cardiac output.
- **The beat after a premature beat (post-extrasystolic)**: a long pause (more filling) plus post-extrasystolic potentiation.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body:
### Manoeuvre vs lesion

| Manoeuvre | Main effect | HCM (obstructive) | MVP | AS | MR | VSD | AR | MS | TR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Inspiration | More right-heart filling | No change or softer | Little change | No change or softer | No change or softer | No change | No change or softer | No change or softer | **Louder** (Carvallo) |
| Valsalva strain | Less preload | **Louder** | **Click earlier, murmur longer** | Softer | Softer | Softer | Softer | Softer | Softer (recovers first on release) |
| Standing | Less preload | **Louder** | **Click earlier, murmur longer** | Softer | Softer or no change | Softer | Softer | Softer | Softer |
| Squatting | More preload and afterload | **Softer** | **Click later, murmur shorter** | Louder | Louder | Louder | Louder | Louder | Louder |
| Passive leg raise | More preload | **Softer** | **Click later, murmur shorter** | Louder | Louder or no change | Louder or no change | Louder or no change | Louder | Louder |
| Handgrip | More afterload | **Softer** | Click later, murmur shorter (may be louder: more afterload) | Softer or no change | **Louder** | **Louder** | **Louder** | Louder (higher rate and output) | No change |
| Amyl nitrite | Less afterload, then more flow | **Louder** | Click earlier, murmur longer | **Louder** | **Softer** | **Softer** | **Softer** | **Louder** | Louder (more venous return) |

[[figure:pe-phono-hcm-valsalva]]

**Right-sided lesions:** TR, PS, PR and TS all increase on inspiration. The **pulmonary ejection click** is the exception: it gets softer on inspiration (the higher RV diastolic pressure partly opens the valve before systole).

**Other lesions with amyl nitrite:** MS and the flow murmurs get **louder** (tachycardia, more flow); the **Austin Flint** murmur gets **softer** (less AR), which separates it from true MS.
sections.title: Murmur

sections.body:
**Why HCM goes the "wrong way":** the obstruction is **dynamic**, between the hypertrophied septum and the mitral leaflet drawn forward in systole (SAM). Anything that makes the LV cavity **smaller** (less preload: Valsalva, standing, nitrates, dehydration) or **lowers afterload** (amyl nitrite, vasodilators) or increases contractility narrows the outflow tract further: more gradient, louder murmur. Squatting, leg raise and handgrip enlarge the cavity and soften it. In AS the obstruction is **fixed**, so the murmur simply follows flow: more preload -> louder.

**Why MVP moves:** a smaller LV lets the redundant leaflets prolapse **earlier** in systole, so the click moves towards S1 and the murmur lengthens; a larger LV delays prolapse.

**Afterload separates regurgitant from ejection murmurs:** handgrip and arterial occlusion make MR, VSD and AR louder (more backward flow) and soften HCM; amyl nitrite does the opposite.

**The post-extrasystolic beat:** the AS murmur gets **louder** after a pause, while the MR murmur hardly changes (the extra volume leaks into the low-pressure atrium either way). In obstructive HCM the post-extrasystolic beat has a **louder murmur but a smaller pulse pressure** (more obstruction): the **Brockenbrough-Braunwald-Morrow sign**, seen best on simultaneous catheter pressures.
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
- **Squatting makes HCM softer and AS louder**: the classic discriminator. Standing and Valsalva do the opposite.
- **MVP and HCM move together** with preload; distinguish them by the click and the site.
- Handgrip **softens** HCM (more afterload) but **increases** MR, VSD and AR.
- Amyl nitrite **increases** AS and HCM but **decreases** MR, VSD, AR and Austin Flint.
- Do not use inspiration to call a murmur left-sided: only an **increase** on inspiration is informative (right-sided).
- Valsalva needs a proper strain (about 40 mmHg for 10-15 s); a weak effort changes nothing.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Systolic murmur louder on standing and during Valsalva, softer on squatting" -> obstructive HCM.
- "Click moves closer to S1 on standing" -> mitral valve prolapse.
- "Systolic murmur louder with handgrip, softer with amyl nitrite" -> MR or VSD.
- "Pansystolic murmur at the LLSB louder on inspiration" -> TR (Carvallo sign).
- "Apical rumble softer after amyl nitrite in a patient with severe AR" -> Austin Flint murmur.
- "Louder murmur but smaller pulse after a premature beat" -> HCM (Brockenbrough-Braunwald-Morrow sign).
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **Less preload (Valsalva, standing)**: HCM louder, MVP earlier/longer, everything else softer.
- **More preload (squatting, leg raise)**: HCM softer, MVP later/shorter, AS and the rest louder.
- **More afterload (handgrip, arterial occlusion)**: MR, VSD, AR louder; HCM softer.
- **Less afterload (amyl nitrite)**: AS and HCM louder; MR, VSD, AR, Austin Flint softer; MS louder.
- **Inspiration**: right-sided lesions louder (Carvallo); pulmonary click softer.
